name: Lengthened partials / stretch training

lead: Lengthened partials are repetitions done only through the stretched portion of a lift, for example the bottom half of a curl or fly. Lifters use them to load the muscle where it is most elongated and get more growth in that muscle.

Hypertrophy overviews report that full range of motion, especially at elongated muscle lengths, is described as enhancing growth more than partial range, and that partial-range training at longer muscle lengths is also said to promote hypertrophy, possibly through muscle damage. The sources consulted do not summarise dedicated trials of lengthened partials.

paras: Lifters add them as extra reps at the end of a set or as the main way of performing exercises that load the muscle hard when stretched, such as curls, flyes and calf raises. They are used within a normal split and progressive overload plan.
Heavy loading in stretched positions can stress joints and connective tissue, as with other resistance training. No technique-specific harm data were identified.

angle.text: Lifters train only the stretched part of a rep, such as the bottom of a curl or fly, to build more muscle in that area. Keeping tension high when the muscle is elongated is thought to raise the growth stimulus. Hypertrophy overviews describe training at long muscle lengths as promoting growth, though dedicated trials are not summarised here.

lead: Lengthened partials are repetitions performed only in the stretched portion of an exercise, such as the bottom half of a curl, fly or pulldown, rather than through the full range of motion. Lifters use them to put the most tension on a muscle when it is at its longest, with the aim of building more muscle, for example wider shoulders, a thicker upper chest or fuller arms, which many pursue as part of a stronger physique.

The Wikipedia hypertrophy article reports that full range of motion, particularly at elongated muscle lengths, is described as enhancing growth more than partial range, and that partial-range training at long lengths is also said to promote hypertrophy, possibly through muscle damage.[1]

A 2025 randomized within-participant trial in 30 resistance-trained adults compared lengthened partials with full-range repetitions over eight weeks of upper-body training and reported similar gains in elbow flexor and extensor thickness and lat pulldown 10-rep max between the two conditions.[2]

paras: Lifters either finish a set with extra partial reps in the lengthened range or build whole sets from them. Proponents link the approach to the idea that muscles grow well when loaded at long lengths.[1] Exercises that lend themselves to it include leg extensions, curls, flies and pulldowns; T Nation members describe adding lengthened partials to leg extensions and to a physique program aimed at wider delts, a thicker upper chest and fuller triceps.[3][4]
Reviews of muscle hypertrophy describe mechanical tension as the currently accepted driver of growth and note that exercise at long muscle lengths is described as beneficial.[1]

In the 2025 PeerJ trial, 30 resistance-trained participants trained each arm with a different range of motion, lengthened partials or full range, for eight weeks. Gains in muscle thickness and 10-rep max were similar, with Bayesian analysis supporting no difference, and the authors concluded that emphasising the stretched position, whether through full range or lengthened partials, is the common factor for size.[2][5]

On T Nation the technique is discussed both enthusiastically and skeptically. One poster calls lengthened partials the latest science-based training fad, while others report using them in their own logs.[6][3][4]

One randomized trial directly compares lengthened partials with full-range training in trained participants and found similar muscle thickness and strength-endurance gains.[2][5] Reviews of resistance training and stretching examine range-of-motion improvements more broadly.[7]

lore.intro: Lengthened partials spread through lifting communities as research on training at long muscle lengths became popular; T Nation threads show lifters trying them and others questioning the trend.[6][3][4]
